redizajn-sajta.title: Website redesign: when it is time and how to keep your search rankings
redizajn-sajta.excerpt: The signs that a website needs a redesign and when targeted fixes are enough, where to start, what breaks search rankings and how to keep them, how to launch the updated site — and what it costs.
redizajn-sajta.lead: A redesign usually begins with the question "what will the new design look like" and ends with "where did the enquiries go". The new site looks better than the old one, but a month later it turns out half the pages have dropped out of search and the forms are losing requests. Here we look at when a redesign is really needed, where to start, what most often breaks search rankings, and how to carry out the update so the site becomes not just better-looking but more useful.
redizajn-sajta.metaTitle: Website redesign: when you need it and how to keep SEO
redizajn-sajta.metaDescription: When a website needs a redesign and when fixes are enough, where to start, what breaks search rankings, how to keep traffic at launch and what it costs.

sections.heading: When a redesign is really needed
body: The site is awkward on a phone. Most visitors today arrive on mobile, and if the text is tiny on a small screen, the buttons are hard to tap and the form slides off the edge, no amount of content will save it.

The business has changed and the site hasn't. There are new services, a different audience, the company has outgrown the niche it started in — and the site keeps describing what it was three years ago.

The numbers say the site is losing people. A high share of visitors leaving from the first page, short visits, few enquiries despite decent traffic — a sign that the problem is the site itself, not the advertising.

And the technology holds growth back. The site is slow, the platform is outdated and no longer updated, and adding a new page needs a developer every time. In that case a new design is also a reason to sort out what the site runs on.

sections.heading: When a redesign isn't needed
body: "We're tired of the design" is a weak reason. More often it is the owner who is tired of it, seeing the site every day — not the client opening it for the first time.
A competitor updating their site isn't a reason either. If yours brings in enquiries, their new design takes nothing from you, while a rebuild for the sake of fashion might.
If the problem is traffic or the offer itself, new visuals won't solve it. A beautiful site with no visitors still gets no enquiries, and a weak offer in new packaging is still weak.

Targeted fixes are often enough: a new first screen, a rewritten offer, faster loading, a repaired form, clear prices. That is quicker and cheaper than a full redesign, and the effect can be comparable.

sections.heading: Refresh the visuals, restructure or migrate
body: The word "redesign" covers three different jobs. A visual refresh keeps the structure and the pages and changes the look: fonts, colours, blocks, photos. This is the safest option for search rankings.

Restructuring changes the architecture: which pages exist, how they connect, what a person sees and in what order on the way to an enquiry. It goes deeper and is more useful, but it affects page addresses and texts — and therefore search.
Migrating to a new platform changes what the site runs on. It is often combined with a redesign, which is sensible, but this is where the risks are greatest.
The rule is simple: the deeper the changes, the more detailed the plan for keeping what already works needs to be.

sections.heading: Start with data, not with pictures
body: The first step is finding out what works on the site right now. Which pages bring in visitors from search, and which of them bring in enquiries. They must not be lost, and any conversation about a new structure starts with them.

Next: which queries the site is found by, where people come from, on which devices, on which pages they leave. This is visible in analytics and in the tools for site owners — Google Search Console and Yandex Webmaster.
Session recordings and click maps show what the numbers don't: where people look for a button that isn't there, and how far down a page they read.

And a conversation with the sales team. What questions do clients ask again and again, what convinces them and what stops them? The answers to those questions belong on the site, and the new design should give them a prominent place.

sections.heading: What breaks search rankings
body: Changing addresses without redirects. A search engine knows a page by its address; if the address changes and the old one answers "page not found", the rankings it built up disappear with it.

Deleted pages and cut text. A page that brought in traffic didn't make it into the new structure. Or the text was replaced with beautiful images and three lines — and the search engine has nothing left to show it for.
Lost titles and meta tags. The new template puts the same title on every page by default, and the site vanishes from results for queries it was visible for over the years.

A site closed to search. The test version is blocked from indexing — and that block moves to the live site along with everything else. It is one of the most common and most frustrating launch mistakes.
And speed. Background video, heavy animations and huge images make a site slow, and search engines take loading speed into account.

sections.heading: Page addresses and redirects
body: The best option is not to change addresses unless you have to. If the structure allows the old addresses to be kept, the new page simply takes the old one's place, and the search engine barely notices.

If addresses do change, a mapping table is drawn up: old address to new address, for every page that had traffic or external links. Permanent redirects are set up from it — code 301, which tells the search engine the page has moved for good.
Redirecting everything to the home page is not an option. A search engine treats that almost as a deletion, and a person who followed a link to a specific article lands on the home page and leaves.
After launch the table is checked: every old address must lead to its own new page in a single hop, without chains of several redirects.

sections.heading: Content: keep what works
body: The texts of pages that rank well are carried over in substance. They can be rewritten and shortened, but the topic, the key phrasing and the answers to visitors' questions must stay.
Page titles, descriptions for search results and structured data are carried over and improved, not started from scratch. Especially on pages that already bring in traffic.
Images get descriptions, and new pages get links from existing ones. A search engine finds new sections slowly when they are connected to nothing.

A new design is a good occasion to clear out what isn't needed: outdated news, duplicates and pages with no visitors. But the decision rests on data, not on a hunch, and removed pages that had traffic get redirects too.

sections.heading: Phone first
body: The design is drawn for the phone first and then expanded to the desktop. The other way round works worse: a wide layout has to be squeezed, and on a small screen it turns into a jumble.

Speed is checked on real phones and mobile internet, not on the designer's work computer. Search engines judge it by three measures: how quickly the main content appears, how quickly the page responds to a tap, and whether the layout jumps while it loads.
Animation is good as long as it doesn't get in the way. A pretty entrance for the blocks that makes the enquiry button appear after three seconds costs more than it looks in the presentation.

sections.heading: A design system instead of a set of mock-ups
body: Mock-ups of individual pages go out of date with the very first new page they didn't include. A design system is a set of rules and ready-made components: the grid, fonts, colours, buttons, cards, forms with all their states.

New pages are assembled from these components in hours rather than drawn from scratch over weeks. And a year later the site still looks coherent, not like a collection of pages made in different years by different people.
The file with the mock-ups and the component library stays with the company. Even if another team takes over the site later, it won't have to start from zero.

sections.heading: The test version and the launch
body: The new site is built on a closed test address: password access, indexing blocked. That is also where it is tested on real devices and the whole visitor journey to an enquiry is walked through.

Before launch there is a short checklist: the indexing block is lifted, robots.txt and the sitemap are in place, redirects work, analytics and goals are set up, forms reach the people who handle them.
The launch happens on a quiet day: not on a Friday evening and not at the height of the season. The old version is kept in full, so that if something serious goes wrong it can be restored in minutes.
And straight after launch the site is opened through a client's eyes: the home page, the key services, the form, the phone number in the header, the pages that the advertising leads to.

sections.heading: The first weeks after launch
body: Ranking fluctuations in the first weeks are normal: the search engine needs time to recrawl the site and link the new addresses to the old ones. If the redirects and texts are in place, the rankings return, and often grow.

Search Console and Webmaster reports are checked every day: crawl errors, "not found" pages, pages excluded from search. Every error found is fixed straight away, not saved up for the end of the month.

Results are compared with the period before launch, allowing for seasonality: traffic, enquiries, conversion on the key pages. Without analytics set up in advance there is nothing to compare with, and arguments about whether the redesign succeeded turn into an exchange of impressions.

sections.heading: What it costs and how long it takes
body: Design of up to five pages, with prototypes of the key screens, layouts for phone and tablet and hand-over of the mock-ups to development — from {price:60000} and from two weeks.
A design system: research and user scenarios, up to fifteen screens, grid, typography, colours and a component library with all states — from {price:140000} and from four weeks.
A turnkey site with a custom design, content, integrations and a foundation for search — from {price:150000} and from three weeks.

The technical side for search — titles and meta tags, structured data, checks of indexing, robots.txt and the sitemap — from {price:40000} and from one week. It is worth including in any kind of redesign: it is most often what decides whether the site keeps its rankings.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
body: Starting with mock-ups without looking at the analytics. The new design turns out beautiful but is built around pages nobody needs, and it loses the ones that brought in clients.
Changing addresses without a redirect table. The shortest route to a traffic collapse after launch.
Throwing out the text for the sake of a "clean" design. Minimalism is fine as long as the page answers the visitor's questions. When it doesn't, both the visitor and the search engine leave.
Launching the site with indexing blocked. A one-line mistake that is sometimes noticed only weeks later, when the traffic has already fallen.
Changing everything at once — design, texts, structure and platform — and then not understanding what exactly affected the result.

sections.heading: Where to start this week
body: Export from your analytics the twenty pages that bring in the most visitors and enquiries. That is the list of what the new site must keep.
Look in Search Console or Webmaster at which queries the site is found by. You will also see which ones it isn't found by, although it should be.
Open the site on your own phone and walk the client's path: from the first screen to a submitted enquiry. Write down every place where you had to search, wait or zoom in on the text.

And state the goal in one sentence: what should change after the redesign — more enquiries, a different audience, less manual work on the site. That sentence is how you will later tell whether the project succeeded.

takeaways: A redesign is needed when the site is awkward on a phone, the business has changed, the numbers show visitors being lost or the technology holds growth back. Being tired of the design or a competitor's update are weak reasons, and targeted fixes are often enough.
The work starts with data: which pages bring traffic and enquiries, which queries the site is found by, where visitors leave, what clients ask.
Search rankings are broken by changed addresses without redirects, deleted pages and texts, lost meta tags, indexing left blocked after launch, and slow loading.
If addresses change, every page with traffic gets a permanent 301 redirect to its new version, not to the home page.
Design for the phone first, build from a design system, launch on a quiet day with the old version kept, and check Search Console and Webmaster for errors every day in the first weeks.

Design of up to five pages — from {price:60000} and two weeks; a design system — from {price:140000}; a turnkey site with a custom design — from {price:150000}; the technical side for search — from {price:40000}.

uchetnaya-sistema-dlya-biznesa.title: A business system instead of spreadsheets: when Excel stops coping and what to implement
uchetnaya-sistema-dlya-biznesa.excerpt: The signs that it is time to swap spreadsheets for a system, how an ERP differs from a CRM, how to choose between an off-the-shelf product and custom development, migrate the data and launch the system so people actually use it — and what it costs.
uchetnaya-sistema-dlya-biznesa.lead: Almost every business starts keeping records in spreadsheets, and for a long time that is the right call: fast, free and clear to everyone. But there comes a point when the spreadsheets eat more time than they save, and nobody can answer a simple question like "how much did we make on this client" without two days of reconciliation. Here we look at how to tell that point has come, which system to choose, how to migrate the data and launch without chaos — and what it all costs.
uchetnaya-sistema-dlya-biznesa.metaTitle: Business system instead of Excel: choice, rollout, costs
uchetnaya-sistema-dlya-biznesa.metaDescription: When spreadsheets should give way to a business system, how it differs from a CRM, how to choose a product, migrate the data and launch without chaos.

sections.heading: Signs that spreadsheets are no longer coping
body: Versions drift apart. The sales manager has one orders sheet, the warehouse another, the accountant a third, and each considers their own to be the truth. Before any important decision they have to be reconciled first — by hand, and with mistakes.

The same thing is recorded in different ways. A client under three spellings, a product under two names, a supplier with a typo in their company details. A report on a client or a product has to be assembled with searching and guesswork.

The stock level in the spreadsheet doesn't match the warehouse, and the monthly sales report takes two days to put together. The formulas everything rests on are understood by one person, and their holiday is a risk for the whole company.
And access works on an all-or-nothing basis. Anyone the file was forwarded to can see purchase prices, and there is no way to tell who changed a figure, or when.

sections.heading: A business system and a CRM are not the same thing
body: A business system, or ERP, keeps track of what happens to goods, money and resources: purchasing, the warehouse, sales, production, settlements with counterparties and often accounting too. Everything lives in one database and moves through documents: a posted shipment reduces stock by itself and increases what the client owes by itself.

A CRM keeps track of clients and deals up to the sale: enquiries, calls, correspondence, the pipeline. It usually has no stock levels or cost prices, and trying to run a warehouse in a CRM is like running sales in accounting software.

Many companies need both, connected by an integration: a deal closed in the CRM becomes an order in the business system; goods shipped show up as a status for the sales manager. The key is to decide in advance which system is responsible for which data, so the truth doesn't split in two again.

sections.heading: Process first, system second
body: A system cements a process, whatever that process is. If an order passes through five pairs of hands today and gets lost in two places, after the rollout it will get lost in two places in the software — only at greater cost.

So you start with a description: how an order moves from enquiry to payment, how goods come in, how money is counted, who enters what and who uses what. A one-page diagram and a list of the documents the company cannot work without are enough.
Often this stage alone reveals that half the spreadsheets exist only because two others aren't connected. And that some problems are solved by an agreement within the company, not by software.

sections.heading: Off-the-shelf product, industry solution or custom development
body: Off-the-shelf systems — 1C, Odoo, SAP Business One, Microsoft Dynamics and dozens of others — already handle standard operations: warehouse, purchasing, sales, money. Rolling them out is faster and cheaper, and specialists are easy to find.

Industry solutions — for restaurants, healthcare, manufacturing, construction — arrive already set up for the specifics, so there is less to configure. The flip side is less freedom if your process differs from the industry standard.

Custom development is justified when the process is unique and is exactly what sets you apart from competitors, while an off-the-shelf system would have to be reshaped. It costs more at the start, but the system does exactly what you need.
A simple rule: if the customisations outweigh the standard functionality, the wrong product was chosen — it is cheaper to take another one or to build your own.

sections.heading: Cloud or your own server
body: A cloud version launches faster: no server is needed, the provider handles updates and backups, and people can work from anywhere. You pay a subscription, and the cost is easy to calculate in advance.

Your own server gives more freedom to customise and full control over the data, but administration, updates and backups become your job. That makes sense when there are many customisations or when data cannot be kept with a third-party provider.

Before choosing, two questions are worth checking. Does the cloud version allow the customisations and integrations you need? And what do the laws of your country require about where client and employee data is stored?

sections.heading: How to choose: questions to ask of a system
body: Does it cover your five main processes out of the box, without customisation? This should be checked in a demo with your data and your scenarios, not in the vendor's presentation.
Does it connect to what you already have: the website, marketplaces, the bank, the till, telephony, the CRM? A ready-made exchange with the service you need saves weeks of development.

What does it cost over three years, not in the first month: licences or subscription, implementation, customisations, support, training new staff? A cheap system with expensive customisations often ends up costing more than an expensive one that has everything.
And can you take your data with you? A system that won't let you export reference data and transaction history in an open format ties you to it more tightly than any contract.

sections.heading: Data migration is the most underestimated part
body: Reference data — products, clients, suppliers — is cleaned before migration, not after. Duplicates, different spellings, obsolete items: whatever ends up in the new system stays there for a long time and spoils the reports from day one.

Balances are migrated as of a specific date — usually the start of a month or quarter — and checked against reality: the warehouse against a stocktake, settlements against confirmations from counterparties. It is better to find a discrepancy before the launch than in the very first report.

Transaction history is migrated to an agreed depth. Sometimes balances and open deals are enough; sometimes a year of sales is needed for analytics. Migrating everything for ten years rarely pays off: old data can stay in an archive and be viewed there.
In practice, cleaning the data often takes longer than configuring the system itself. That is normal — and worth building into the plan from the very beginning.

sections.heading: Permissions and roles
body: A salesperson needs one screen — the order and stock levels; an accountant needs the whole finance module; a manager needs reports. The less irrelevant information an employee sees, the faster they work and the fewer mistakes they make.

Permissions also settle questions of trust. Who sees purchase prices and margins, who can change prices, who deletes documents and who backdates them — this is settled by configuring roles, not by asking people to "be more careful".
Unlike a spreadsheet, a system remembers who changed what and when. An argument along the lines of "I didn't enter that" is settled in a minute, and a backdated document is visible straight away.

sections.heading: Integrations: the system doesn't live alone
body: Orders from the website and marketplaces, bank statements, till receipts, calls, deals from the CRM — all of it should reach the records on its own. Without integrations, manual re-entry simply moves from the spreadsheet into the system, and half the benefit is lost.

For every exchange it is decided in advance what is transferred, in which direction, how often and which system is the master. Stock levels on the website that update once a day mean orders for goods that are already gone.
Integrations need watching. An exchange that quietly stopped working on Friday is discovered on Monday as a hundred orders that never arrived. Monitoring with alerts costs far less.

sections.heading: Launching one area at a time
body: Not everything is launched at once. First one area — sales, for example — then the warehouse, then purchasing or production. Each next stage takes the previous one's mistakes into account, and employees don't drown in changes.
The switchover date is set at the start of a period: a month or a quarter. That makes balances easier to reconcile and avoids splitting one reporting period between two ways of keeping records.
Running the spreadsheets and the system in parallel is acceptable for a week or two, no longer. Any longer and the company has two truths again, and employees choose the familiar one.
The first month-end close in the new system happens with support at hand. That is when the reports, reconciliations and documents nobody touches on ordinary days come to the surface.

sections.heading: People and training
body: Training is done by role, not as one general lecture. A warehouse worker doesn't need to know how the month is closed, and an accountant doesn't need to know how an order is picked. Each person gets their own screens and their own operations, on their real tasks.
Instructions are written for your processes rather than retelling the vendor's manual. A short cheat sheet on "how to process a return" is more useful than two hundred pages of documentation.

The company needs a key user — an employee who knows the system better than anyone, answers colleagues' questions and gathers requests. Without one, every small thing turns into a ticket for the contractor.
And the old spreadsheets are closed. "Let's keep them just in case" almost always ends with the work quietly drifting back into Excel.

sections.heading: What it costs and how long it takes
body: Rolling out a standard configuration with a process review, migration of reference data and balances, permission setup and training — from {price:150000} and from four weeks.

With data migrated from previous systems, documents and reports configured, integration with the website and the bank, and support through the first reporting period — from {price:290000} and from seven weeks. This is the most common option.
Several legal entities and warehouses, the till, telephony, marketplaces, customisations for your processes — from {price:550000} and from twelve weeks.

Individual changes to a system that is already running — a report, a print form, an export — from {price:25000} and from three days. An integration with one service — from {price:50000} and from one week. Licences or the subscription for the system itself are paid separately.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
body: Buying a system before describing the processes. Choosing from a presentation without your own scenarios is the most common route to customisations that cost more than the licence.
Migrating the junk. Duplicates and errors from the spreadsheets, carried over as they are, make the new system as unreliable as the old one — only more expensive to fix.
Launching everything at once. When sales, the warehouse and accounting all change at the same time, nobody knows where to look at the first problem, and nothing works.
Customising it beyond recognition. A system with half of its standard functionality rewritten stops receiving updates and is frozen on its current version for good.
Not appointing an owner. Without someone responsible inside the company, within a year the system is surrounded by workaround spreadsheets, and everything is back where it started.

sections.heading: Where to start this week
body: List the spreadsheets the company keeps its records in, and note who maintains each one and who uses it. That is a map of what needs replacing.
Write down three reports the director would like to see every week that are currently put together by hand. That is the main criterion by which you will later judge whether the rollout succeeded.

Draw the path of one order — from enquiry to payment and shipment — with every spreadsheet and person it passes through. The places where data is retyped by hand are exactly what the system should remove.

And count how many hours a month go on reconciliations, summary tables and hunting for errors. Multiplied by the cost of an hour, they show how much the company is already paying for not having a system.

takeaways: It is time to swap spreadsheets for a system when versions drift apart, reference data is full of duplicates, stock levels don't match the warehouse and the monthly report takes days to assemble.

A business system tracks goods, money and resources; a CRM tracks clients and deals up to the sale. Many companies need both, connected by an integration, with responsibility for each kind of data agreed in advance.

An off-the-shelf product is faster and cheaper, an industry solution fits the specifics more closely, custom development suits a unique process. If the customisations outweigh the standard functionality, the choice was wrong.
Cleaning and migrating the data often takes longer than configuration: reference data is cleaned before migration, and balances are reconciled as of the switchover date.
Launch one area at a time from the start of a period, limit parallel work in spreadsheets to a couple of weeks, train by role and appoint a key user inside the company.

A standard configuration — from {price:150000} and four weeks; with data migration and integrations — from {price:290000}; complex projects — from {price:550000}. Customisations — from {price:25000}, integrations — from {price:50000}.

importozameshchenie-po.title: Replacing foreign software in Russia: where to start and how to keep working
importozameshchenie-po.excerpt: Who is required by law to move to Russian software and who has simply run out of time, what to replace first, why projects break on compatibility and on people — and what the move costs.
importozameshchenie-po.lead: For a long time, import substitution was a job for state companies and banks. Now it reaches those the law asks nothing of: licences cannot be renewed, updates no longer arrive, and a client asks what its contractor's systems run on. Here we look at who has to make the move, where to begin, where it usually breaks and what it costs — in a way that lets the company keep working throughout.
importozameshchenie-po.metaTitle: Moving to Russian software: plan, risks and costs
importozameshchenie-po.metaDescription: Who is legally required to switch to Russian software, what to replace first, how to check compatibility, run a pilot and what the move costs.

sections.heading: Who the law obliges and who it doesn't
body: The strictest rules apply to critical information infrastructure, or CII. That covers banks, telecoms, energy, transport, healthcare, industry and several other sectors. Since 1 September 2025 the law has directly required significant CII facilities to be moved to Russian software from the official register.

The baseline deadline for significant facilities is 1 January 2028. For certain cases the government is discussing later dates — for instance, where no Russian replacement exists yet. So the deadline for your own system should be checked against the resolution currently in force and your sector's plan, not against a news item from a year ago.

For government bodies and state-owned companies, foreign software on significant facilities has been banned since 1 January 2025. And in procurement they must choose programs from the register whenever a suitable one is there.

The law does not oblige other businesses to switch. But if you supply a state company or bid in tenders, the requirements arrive in the contract: the client is entitled to ask what your systems run on and where its data is kept.

sections.heading: Why companies switch when nobody makes them
body: Licences. Many foreign vendors stopped sales and support in Russia in 2022. Renewing a subscription or buying licences for new employees through official channels is often impossible, and grey schemes mean paying with no guarantees and no right to demand anything.

Updates. A program without updates works as it did before, but every vulnerability found in it stays open for good. For Windows 10, for example, free security updates ended on 14 October 2025, and with each month such a computer on the network becomes an easier target.

Shutdowns. A cloud service can be switched off with one button on the other side, and this is no longer theory: in 2024 some foreign enterprise services were cut off for Russian organisations at short notice. Mail, calendars and documents in someone else's cloud are the most fragile part of the infrastructure.

And planning. A move started in advance goes in stages and to a plan. A move after a system fails happens over a weekend and however it turns out. The difference in cost between the two is severalfold.

sections.heading: The register of Russian software: why look at it
body: The register is kept by the Ministry of Digital Development and it is public: any program can be looked up by name or rights holder. For those the law obliges, it is the only list of what is allowed — a program outside the register does not legally count as Russian, whatever the developer's company is called.

For everyone else the register is useful as a filter. An entry means the rights holder is Russian, the product can be bought officially, and support can be obtained under a contract and paid for in roubles.

But an entry in the register does not mean the program will suit you. The register says nothing about whether it will open your files, work with your label printer or have enough features for your accounting team. That can only be checked on your own tasks.

Certificates from FSTEC and the FSB are a separate matter. Certified editions are needed where information protection rules demand them: in government systems, on significant CII facilities, in some systems holding personal data. Whether you need them is decided before purchase: such an edition costs more and is updated more slowly.

sections.heading: Where to start: an inventory
body: The move does not begin with choosing an operating system. It begins with a list. Which programs are installed on computers and servers, who actually uses them, which licences there are and until what date, what depends on what.

The list usually turns out longer than expected. Spreadsheet macros without which the month cannot be closed. Software for a machine tool written in 2011. A banking client with its key on a USB stick. An add-on to the accounting system whose author nobody remembers.

Hardware gets its own line: printers, scanners, tills, data collection terminals, electronic signature tokens. The new system needs a driver, and it is better to learn there isn't one before buying licences than on the day the warehouse moves.

The result of the inventory is a table where every program has an owner, a rating of importance and a decision: replace, leave as it is, or drop. The third option comes up more often than you'd think: a noticeable share of what is installed has not been used by anyone for a long time.

sections.heading: What to replace first
body: Not everything at once, and not what is most visible. The order is set by risk, not by habit: first whatever faces the internet and is no longer updated.

The first wave is mail, remote access, security tools and backups. A breached mail server, or ransomware with no working backup, stops the whole company, while replacing these touches employees' habits the least.

The second is servers and what runs on them: the user directory, file storage, virtualisation, databases. Technically this is the hardest part, and the least noticeable to people if it is done carefully.
The third is workstations: the operating system and the office suite. There is less technical risk here and more human risk, so they are moved department by department and only after a pilot.

Highly specialised programs come last — or never. If there is no replacement, it is more honest to leave a few machines on the old system in an isolated network segment than to halt production for the sake of ticking a box.

sections.heading: What replaces what, class by class
body: Operating systems. Astra Linux, RED OS, ALT and ROSA are all Linux-based and all in the register. They differ in the software bundled with them, the tools for managing a fleet of machines and whether certified editions exist.

Office and mail. MyOffice and R7-Office open familiar documents and spreadsheets; the difficulties begin with macros and complex layouts. For mail and calendars there are both server products and cloud services from Russian providers.

The user directory. What Active Directory does in the Windows world: accounts, groups, policies. The replacements are ALD Pro, RED ADM and Alt Domain. For a while they can run alongside the old domain, and that is a normal way to migrate.

Virtualisation, databases, backup, video calls. Each class has several mature products, and the choice should rest not on advertising but on what already works at companies of your size with your set of systems.

sections.heading: Where the move breaks: compatibility
body: On programs that do not exist for the new system. There are three options. Find an equivalent. Run the old program in a compatibility layer — some Windows applications work that way, but not all and not always reliably. Or leave an island: a few machines or a terminal server on the old system that people log into only for that program.

On files. A simple document will open anywhere. A twenty-sheet spreadsheet with macros, pivot tables and links to other files may not. Such files are found during the inventory and checked one by one: some are rewritten, some are moved into the accounting system, where they belonged long ago.

On electronic signatures and banks. The cryptographic provider, the browser plug-in, the banking client, filing reports — each has its own requirements for the system and the browser. Almost all of it exists for Russian operating systems, but it is not set up in five minutes, which is why accounting is checked first.

And on the accounting system. The 1C server and the database beneath it move well, but every customised configuration has external add-ons, data exchanges and print forms. Listing them is a mandatory part of the survey.

sections.heading: Domain and mail: what the user never sees
body: Changing the user directory is the most critical part of the project. Logging into a computer, access to folders, printers, mail and often the accounting system all hang on it. So the new directory is first deployed next to the old one, and departments are moved into it one at a time.

Access rights are worth rebuilding rather than copying. Over the years they have accumulated former employees, shared folders "for everyone" and exceptions nobody can explain. A migration is a rare moment when order can be restored along the way.

Mail is moved so that nobody loses a single message: mailboxes, calendars, shared addresses, forwarding rules, archives. For a while the old and new servers work together, and mail arrives whether an employee has been moved yet or not.
And all this time a backup must be working — of both the old environment and the new. One proven by a restore, not merely configured.

sections.heading: A pilot with real people
body: Before the mass rollout, the new environment is set up for 5–10 employees from different departments. Not the most loyal ones and not the IT staff, but ordinary people: an accountant, a sales manager, a warehouse worker, a director.
The pilot lasts from two to four weeks and has to cover the end of a month. That is when the reports, reconciliations and print forms that nobody touches on ordinary days come to the surface.

The outcome of a pilot is not "everything works" but a list: what got in the way, what turned out to be incompatible, what took extra time. Settings and instructions are refined from it, and sometimes the chosen product is changed — which is far cheaper than changing it after buying it for the whole company.
The main technical result is a workstation image. When the system, programs, settings and access rights are deployed to a computer automatically, moving a department takes a day rather than a week.

sections.heading: Moving in stages, with a rollback plan
body: Departments are moved one by one, starting with those that have the simplest set of programs. Each stage takes the previous one's mistakes into account, and a mixed fleet — part of the company on the new system, part on the old — is a normal state for several months.

Every stage has a maintenance window and a rollback plan. The old environment is not switched off until the new one has been checked: if something goes wrong, the department returns to its previous setup within hours instead of being restored from backups over days.
Critical steps are rehearsed. Moving a database or a mail server is first done on a copy, with the time measured and the result checked. On the night of the real move there should be no surprises.
After each stage come a couple of weeks of observation: load, errors, requests from employees. The next department starts when the previous one has stopped calling.

sections.heading: People: why projects fail on something other than technology
body: An employee for whom everything looks different on Monday morning, and to whom nothing was explained, has every right to be angry. Most failed migrations are not about incompatible software but about a department that quietly goes back to the old way because the new one gets in the way of work.

Simple things help. Warn people in advance and explain why. Hand out a short cheat sheet: where the files are now, how to print, how to open an old document. In the first week, seat someone nearby who answers questions straight away.

Don't change everything in one day. A new system, a new office suite and new mail at once are three stresses instead of one. The office suite and mail can be changed earlier, while still on the old system, and then the change of the operating system itself passes almost unnoticed.
And start with the managers. If the director has stayed on the old laptop "as an exception", everyone understands that the project is optional.

sections.heading: What it costs and how long it takes
body: Moving workstations to a Russian operating system, with a compatibility audit, a pilot, a single image and migration of users' data — from {price:150000} and from three weeks. With domain infrastructure, policies, mass deployment by department and training — from {price:280000} and from five weeks.

Moving the server side — databases and mail, with a rehearsal on a copy and replacement of systems that are out of support — from {price:220000} and from five weeks. A move with no interruption to work and a staged transfer of departments — from {price:400000} and from eight weeks.

Licences are counted separately, and what is worth counting is not the purchase price but three years of ownership: the licences themselves, vendor support, training, the administrator's time. Often what surfaced during the inventory costs more than the software: rewritten macros and new peripherals.

As for timing, a company with 30–50 workstations and one office goes from inventory to the last department in three to six months. It is rarely faster, and almost always at the expense of a skipped pilot.
After the move the system needs an owner: updates, backups, new employees, requests. Support under an agreement with a fixed response time starts from {price:30000/mo}.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
body: Starting with the purchase. Licences for the whole company bought before the pilot are the most expensive way to find out that the product doesn't fit.
Moving everyone over a weekend. On Monday the administrator will have a hundred equally urgent requests, and the company will not have a single department working normally.
Forgetting about peripherals and macros. The system went in without a single error, yet the warehouse cannot print labels and accounting cannot close the month.
Changing the system but not how it is managed. A hundred computers on a new OS with no directory, policies or centralised updates are the same patchwork as before, only unfamiliar.
Leaving no way back. The old environment was switched off on the day of the move — and the very first serious problem turns from a rollback into an outage.

sections.heading: Where to start this week
body: Make a list of the programs and services the company uses every day, and mark which of them are no longer updated and which live in a foreign cloud. That is a risk map, and it is useful even if the move begins a year from now.
Check the backups — by restoring, not by reading the report. It is the only insurance in case one of the marked systems fails before its turn comes.
Pick five people from different departments for the future pilot and ask which programs and files they cannot work without. The answers almost always differ from what the administrator knows.

And appoint someone responsible. Not for the technology but for the project as a whole: deadlines, the order of departments, decisions on disputed programs. Without that person the move drags on for years and stops at the first unhappy department.

takeaways: The law requires significant critical-infrastructure facilities (baseline deadline: 1 January 2028), government bodies and state-owned companies to move to Russian software. For other businesses the requirements more often come from clients.

Companies switch without being obliged to: licences cannot be renewed, there are no security updates, a foreign cloud service may be cut off, and an emergency move costs several times more than a planned one.
Start with an inventory, not with choosing a system. Mail, remote access, security and backups are replaced first, then servers, then workstations.

The move breaks on compatibility: specialised programs, macros, electronic signatures, peripherals. There are three ways to handle what is incompatible — an equivalent, a compatibility layer, or an island on the old system.
A pilot with 5–10 ordinary employees, a department-by-department move and an old environment that is not switched off until the new one is checked are what separate a planned project from an outage.

Moving workstations to a Russian OS — from {price:150000} and three weeks; moving servers and mail — from {price:220000}; support after the move — from {price:30000/mo}. A company with 30–50 workstations covers the whole path in three to six months.

ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.title: AI agents for business: what you can trust them with today
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.excerpt: How an agent differs from a chatbot, which tasks companies already hand over to one, why a model makes mistakes with confidence and how to catch them, what to do about personal data — and what a rollout costs.
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.lead: A year ago, AI in a company meant a chat window that employees pasted emails into. Today it increasingly means an agent that reads an enquiry by itself, finds the answer in the knowledge base, creates a deal in the CRM and calls in a person when it isn't sure. Here we look at what such an agent can really be trusted with, where it gets things wrong, how it works under the hood and what bringing one in costs.
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.metaTitle: AI agents for business: tasks, risks and costs
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.metaDescription: What an AI agent is and how it differs from a chatbot, which tasks it takes on, how to handle model errors, what 152-FZ requires and what a rollout costs.

sections.heading: Agent, assistant, chatbot: what's the difference
body: An ordinary chatbot follows a script: buttons, branches, answers written in advance. It doesn't understand a question that doesn't match any of the buttons, and honestly replies "I didn't understand".

An assistant built on a language model understands free text and answers in its own words. But it only answers: it does nothing in your systems, which means all the work after the answer is still left to a person.

An agent is the next step. It is given tools: find an order by its number, check what is left in stock, create a deal in the CRM, book a client into a free slot. The model decides for itself which tool to call and in what order, gets the result and carries on until the task is done or until it is time to call in a person.

For a business, the difference is fundamental. An assistant saves time on wording an answer. An agent closes the whole enquiry — and that is exactly why an agent's mistake costs more: it didn't just give an inaccurate answer, it did something.

sections.heading: What companies already hand over to an agent
body: First-line support. Opening hours, delivery terms, order status, returns, warranty — questions whose answers already sit in your documents and systems. The agent answers instantly, around the clock, and passes anything complicated to an employee with the context already gathered.

Sorting incoming messages. Emails, enquiries from the website, messenger messages: the agent works out what each one is — an order, a complaint, a question, spam — pulls out the contact details and the gist, creates a card in the CRM and sends it to the right department. A manager starts the day not by sorting the inbox but with a ready-made list of tasks.

Working with documents. Invoices, contracts, completion certificates, specifications: the agent finds the fields it needs, checks the amounts against the invoice in the accounting system and flags any discrepancies. What used to be typed in by hand now only needs checking.

Helping sales. A draft commercial proposal from a brief, an answer to a typical objection, a short summary of the correspondence with a client before a call. The decision stays with the manager, but the blank page disappears.

Internal knowledge search. Policies, instructions, past projects: an employee asks in their own words and gets an answer with a link to the document. This is the most underrated scenario — it has no external customers, but it saves every new employee hours every week.

sections.heading: Where an agent still falls short
body: Where a mistake costs more than the savings. Decisions about money, legal wording, medical and financial advice — the agent can prepare a draft, but a person has to sign it off.

Where there is no data. The agent doesn't know your prices, lead times and exceptions until you give them to it. If the answer lives only in the head of an experienced manager, the agent will guess it — and guess plausibly.

Where every case is unique. A complex deal with negotiations, a conflict with a client, a non-standard order. An agent needs repetitive tasks: on rare ones it makes mistakes more often and brings less benefit.

And where there is no process. If enquiries get lost today because nobody is responsible for sorting them, an agent won't help — it will neatly file the enquiries away where nobody looks. Process first, automation second.

sections.heading: Why a model is confidently wrong
body: A language model doesn't look the answer up in a database — it continues the text in the most probable way. When it doesn't have the fact it needs, it fills in a plausible one: a tariff that doesn't exist, an invented delivery time, a contract clause that isn't there. And it says all this in the same confident tone as the truth.

The main cure is grounding. The agent answers not "from memory" but from the documents it has found: first a search of your knowledge base, then an answer based strictly on what was found, with a link to the source. If nothing turns up, the right answer is "I don't know, I'm passing this to a specialist", and that has to be written explicitly into the agent's instructions.

The second is narrow boundaries. An online shop's support agent has no business discussing politics or giving health advice. The more precisely you describe what it does and what it doesn't do, the less room there is for invention.

The third is verification wherever the answer is structured. If the agent has pulled the total and the tax ID (INN) from an invoice, they can be checked against the accounting system automatically. If it has filled in a card in the CRM, the required fields are checked by code, not by hope.
There will still be mistakes. The goal is not zero mistakes but mistakes that are rare, visible and cheap: ones that reach a person rather than a client.

sections.heading: Where an agent gets its knowledge
body: Most often, from your knowledge base: instructions, policies, price lists, answers to frequently asked questions, past correspondence. The documents are cut into fragments, and for each question the agent finds the most relevant pieces and answers from them. This approach is called RAG — retrieval-augmented generation.

Fine-tuning a model on your data is needed less often than it seems. It changes the style and manner, but it is poor at adding facts: prices and lead times that change every month still have to come from up-to-date documents. That is why almost every project starts with a search over the knowledge base and leaves fine-tuning for later — if it is needed at all.

An agent's answers cannot be better than its documents. An outdated price list in the base means an outdated price in the answer. Three versions of the same policy mean three different answers to one question. Putting the knowledge base in order often takes longer than the development itself, and that is normal.

The knowledge base needs an owner: someone who updates the documents when prices and terms change, and looks at which questions the agent couldn't find an answer to. Without that person, six months from now the agent will be politely recounting last year's terms.

sections.heading: Tools: how an agent acts rather than just answers
body: A tool is a function in your system that the agent is allowed to call: find an order, look up free slots, create a request, send a notification. The model sees a description of the tool, decides for itself when to call it and gets the result.

Every tool is a form of access. A support agent needs to read an order's status, but it doesn't need to change prices or delete clients. Permissions are granted at the minimum, exactly for the scenario — just as they are for a new employee on probation.

Irreversible actions require confirmation. Cancelling an order, issuing a refund, sending an email to every client — the agent prepares the action, a person presses the button. It is a little slower and gives you incomparably more peace of mind.

And everything the agent does is logged: which question came in, which tools were called, with which parameters, what the systems returned. Without such a log you can neither investigate a mistake nor prove that there wasn't one.

sections.heading: Human in the loop
body: A good agent knows when to stop. The rules for handing over to a person are written in advance: the client is unhappy, the question is about money, the agent hasn't found an answer, the client explicitly asks for an operator, the conversation is going round in circles.

A handover is not "I'm putting you through to an operator" followed by starting from scratch. The employee receives the enquiry with a summary: who the client is, what they asked, what the agent has already checked and why it stopped. The client doesn't have to explain everything all over again, and that is the main sign that automation has been built for people rather than instead of them.

At the start it helps to keep a person closer: for the first few weeks the agent prepares answers, and an employee checks and sends them. That way you can see where the agent goes wrong, and the knowledge base fills out quickly. Once the quality has settled, the review is kept only for risky topics.

It is worth bringing your employees into the project from the very start. The agent takes the routine off their hands rather than replacing them — and they are the ones who know best which questions keep coming up and where the exceptions are hiding.

sections.heading: Personal data and 152-FZ
body: As soon as an agent handles client enquiries, personal data passes through it: names, phone numbers, addresses, order history. The company remains the operator of that data and is responsible for it under Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, whoever processes it technically.

Sending data to a model run by a foreign service is a cross-border transfer of personal data: Roskomnadzor, Russia's data protection authority, has to be notified in advance, and the service itself must ensure the data is protected. For many companies it is simpler to choose a model from a Russian provider or to deploy an open model on their own server.

Whichever you choose, it is worth masking anything superfluous. A model doesn't need a passport number to answer a question about delivery: data the task can be solved without can be replaced with placeholders before sending and substituted back into the answer.

And a separate point: the logs. Conversations stored for quality control are personal data too. They need a clear retention period and a deletion rule, otherwise within a year the agent's log will become the largest and least protected client database in the company.

sections.heading: How to tell that an agent is working well
body: Before launch, you collect a set of real questions — fifty, a hundred, two hundred — with the correct answers. The agent is tested against it after every change: a new instruction, new documents, a switch of model. Without such an evaluation set, any improvement is a feeling, not a fact.

The metrics are simple. What share of enquiries is closed without a person. How accurate the answers are, judging by spot checks. How often the agent hands the conversation to an employee, and for what reasons. How long it takes to get an answer. And, separately, complaints about the agent's answers.

Quality doesn't stand still after launch. Prices change, new products appear, clients start asking about other things. The questions the agent couldn't find an answer to are the best list of what needs adding to the knowledge base this week.

Compare against how things were before the agent, not against the ideal. If an enquiry sent at the weekend used to get an answer on Monday, and now it gets one within a minute and a correct one nine times out of ten, that is a win — even if the tenth case goes to a person.

sections.heading: What a rollout costs
body: One scenario on one channel — for example, a first-line agent in Telegram that answers from the knowledge base and passes complicated cases to an employee — from {price:90000} and from two weeks. That includes setting it up for your documents, testing it on real questions and the launch.

Several scenarios with integration into the CRM and the knowledge base, quality monitoring and support after launch — from {price:180000} and from three weeks. This is the most common option: the agent not only answers but also creates deals, updates statuses and writes summaries for managers.

End-to-end automation — several connected agents, complex integrations with accounting systems, analytics — from {price:350000} and from five weeks. Here the timeline is most often set not by the agents but by the integrations and the state of the data.

Running costs are a separate line item. Calls to the model are paid for by volume, and at hundreds of enquiries a day this is a noticeable but predictable sum, which you can already see during the trial period. Your own model on your own server costs more at the start and less at high volumes — and, most importantly, the data goes nowhere.

sections.heading: Off-the-shelf service or custom development
body: Off-the-shelf services with an AI bot connect in a day: you upload your documents and get a widget for your website. For simple help on a website that is often enough, and there is no reason to pay for development.

The limitations begin where the agent needs to act in your systems. An off-the-shelf service does what it does: the integrations in its catalogue, its own logic for handing over to a person, its own storage of conversations. If your CRM is custom-built and the data cannot be handed to a third-party service, the boxed product runs out of road quickly.

Custom development costs more at the start, but the agent lives inside your perimeter, works with your systems and obeys your rules: what data goes where, who sees the conversations, what the agent is allowed to do.

The sensible path is to start with a narrow scenario and look at the result. If a boxed product solves the task, you have your solution. If not, you already know which questions come in, where the agent goes wrong and what is missing — and development will start from a ready-made specification.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
body: Starting with the technology rather than the task. "We want AI" is not a task. "We answer 300 identical questions a week and can't keep up at weekends" is a task, and it comes with a ready way to measure the result.

Launching on everything at once. An agent that has to do everything — from support to accounting — does everything equally mediocrely. One narrow scenario brought up to standard is more useful than five half-finished ones.
Not preparing the knowledge base. An agent working from contradictory and outdated documents will give contradictory and outdated answers, and AI will get the blame.
Giving the agent unnecessary permissions. Write access where read access would have done, and actions without confirmation — that is how a single model error turns into an incident.

Not measuring. Without a set of test questions and metrics, a month later it is impossible to say whether the agent has got better or worse, and every argument about quality comes down to impressions.

sections.heading: Where to start
body: Pick one stream of enquiries that repeats most often and eats up time: support questions, sorting incoming enquiries, checking documents. Count how many such enquiries come in each week and how many minutes each one takes — that is your future saving and the project's main metric.

Gather the knowledge the agent will answer from: documents, answers to frequently asked questions, a hundred real enquiries with the correct answers. The agent will be tested against these enquiries both before launch and after.

Describe the boundaries: what the agent does by itself, what it only prepares for a person, and in which cases it must hand the conversation over. One page of such rules matters more than the choice of model.

And launch alongside people. For the first few weeks the agent works under your employees' supervision, the knowledge base is filled out from its misses, and it gets autonomy when the numbers back that up.

takeaways: What sets an agent apart from a chatbot or an assistant is that it acts in your systems: it finds an order, creates a deal, books a client. That is also why its mistakes cost more.
Agents do best at repetitive tasks whose answers are already in documents: first-line support, sorting incoming messages, working with documents, searching internal policies.

A model is confidently wrong when it doesn't know the answer. The cure is answering strictly from the documents found, narrow boundaries, verification of structured data and the right to say "I don't know".
The agent is given minimal permissions, a person confirms irreversible actions, and everything the agent does is logged.
Sending personal data to a foreign model is a cross-border transfer under 152-FZ. The alternative is a Russian provider or your own model on your own server.

One scenario — from {price:90000} and two weeks; several scenarios with CRM and knowledge base — from {price:180000}; end-to-end automation — from {price:350000}. Getting the data in order often takes longer than the development.

svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.title: Custom CRM or off-the-shelf: when a ready-made system is enough and when it isn't
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.excerpt: How an off-the-shelf CRM differs from a custom one — not in features but in consequences: the ceilings boxed systems run into, the decisions you will have to make yourself, what development costs and why the right answer is most often not "or" but "and".
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.lead: The question "buy an off-the-shelf CRM or build your own" is almost never about features. Boxed systems have longer feature lists than any custom build, and on a comparison table the ready-made option always wins. The difference shows up later — when the company's process no longer fits into someone else's data model. Here we look at where that happens, what you will have to decide for yourself and what each path costs.
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.metaTitle: Custom vs off-the-shelf CRM: which to choose, what it costs
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.metaDescription: Off-the-shelf CRM vs custom development: where boxed systems hit a ceiling, what your own CRM costs and when a ready-made one with add-ons is enough.

sections.heading: "We need a CRM" is not yet a requirement
body: Different companies mean different things by the word CRM. For a sales team it is a deal pipeline and call reminders. For an agency, it is tracking projects, hours and invoices. For a service company, it is requests, field staff and a spare parts warehouse. For a manufacturer, it is orders, shipments and a link to the equipment. All four go by the same word, and that is the first reason the "custom or off-the-shelf" comparison goes wrong: people compare not systems but ideas of what a system should do.

So the conversation should start not with choosing a product but with one question: which process do you want to stop keeping in your head and in chat threads? An answer like "we are losing enquiries" points to a pipeline and reminders — exactly what off-the-shelf systems do well. An answer like "we don't know how much we make on a project, because some of the work is billed in dollars, some in roubles, and we pay contractors after the fact" points to accounting that a boxed system doesn't offer in the form you need.

The good news is that the first type of request doesn't need — and shouldn't get — a development project. The bad news is that an off-the-shelf system answers the second type only up to a certain scale, and the boundary is not visible straight away.

sections.heading: What an off-the-shelf system really gives you
body: An off-the-shelf CRM wins where it is usually underestimated: not in its features but in everything around them.

It works today. Not in four weeks, not in three months — tonight, after you sign up and import your contacts from a spreadsheet. For a company that is losing enquiries right now, that outweighs almost any argument about architecture.

It has a mobile app that somebody maintains. Your own app is a separate project with a separate budget, two app stores, update reviews and a release cycle. It is usually left out of the CRM development estimate, and then it turns out that the sales managers need to work from their phones.

It has ready-made integrations with telephony, email, messengers, accounting and cash registers. In your own system each of them is several days of work, plus a further number of days before it stops breaking.

And there are people for it on the job market. A specialist in setting up a widely used CRM can be hired within a week. Someone who knows their way around your own system cannot be hired at all — you can only grow one or keep paying the people who wrote it.
That is a serious list. It is worth giving up only when you get something in return that a boxed system fundamentally does not have.

sections.heading: Three ceilings companies run into
body: The first is the data model. An off-the-shelf system is built around the entities "lead", "contact", "company" and "deal". As long as your process maps onto them, all is well. As soon as an entity appears that this model doesn't have, people start imitating it with whatever is at hand: a project becomes a deal with extra fields, a production stage becomes a pipeline stage, a contractor becomes a contact with a tag. Each such substitution works, but adds a rule that exists only in the team's heads. A year later there are a couple of dozen such rules, and a new employee cannot understand why one deal means a sale and another means an installation stage.

The second is reporting. Reports in off-the-shelf systems are built on the fields the system considers important. When half the meaning lives in custom fields and unwritten agreements, the report starts to lie — not because it calculates incorrectly, but because it calculates the wrong thing. The typical outcome: the data is exported to Excel and counted by hand, which takes you right back to where you started.
The third is the total cost of ownership over several years. More on that separately below, because it is almost always calculated wrongly.
Importantly, none of these ceilings is hit in the first month. All three are a consequence of growth, and that is exactly why "start with an off-the-shelf system" is almost never a mistake.

sections.heading: What "your own CRM" really means
body: Your own system is not "the same thing, just with our fields". It means taking on decisions that, in an off-the-shelf system, someone has already made for you — decisions you didn't know existed, because they are not visible from the interface.

We don't know this from articles: we have our own CRM, which we wrote for ourselves and in which we keep leads, clients, projects, tasks and access credentials. Below are five decisions from it. They look like technical trivia, but each one stands behind a specific mistake that otherwise happens without fail.

sections.heading: Money: why amounts are stored in minor units
body: Money must not be stored as a fractional number. A computer cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly — their sum is not 0.3 but differs from it by a vanishingly small amount. On a single operation you won't notice. Across a few thousand rows the report starts to diverge from reality, first by small change, then by noticeable sums, and nobody can work out where the difference came from.

That is why our system stores every amount as an integer in the currency's smallest unit — kopecks or cents — and whole units appear only on screen and at the moment of entry. The field is called not "amount" but "amount in minor units", on purpose: if the field had silently changed its meaning, every place where someone forgot to update it would show a value a hundred times too large.
In an off-the-shelf CRM you don't need to think about this — it has already been done. In your own, you need to think about it before the first thousand rows appear in the database, not after.

sections.heading: Two currencies you must not add together
body: We bill some of our work in roubles and some in dollars. The obvious solution is to convert everything into one currency and show a grand total. We deliberately don't.

To add roubles to dollars you need an exchange rate. The rate changes. That means the total the report showed yesterday will be different tomorrow — even though not a single deal has changed. A total that changes on its own cannot be reconciled with anything, and trust in it disappears after the first mismatch with the accounts department.

So totals are calculated separately for each currency: two lines instead of one. It is slightly less convenient and completely honest. If a company really needs a single total, then it also needs an exchange rate fixed on the date of each transaction — and that is no longer a field but a separate mechanism, and it has to be designed deliberately.

sections.heading: Passwords: why the server must not see them
body: Access credentials inevitably end up in a CRM: hosting, domains, admin panels of client sites, email. The temptation is to keep them in an ordinary field like everything else. The problem is that the database leaves the server every night as a backup, and every such dump is a ready-made list of all the company's passwords.

Our passwords are encrypted right in the browser, with a key derived from a master passphrase that is never sent to the server. The server stores unreadable text and cannot decrypt it, even in theory. A backup is then worth exactly as much as a random string of characters.

This decision has a price, and you need to know it in advance: nobody can recover a forgotten master passphrase, including the owner of the server. Searching and checking passwords on the server side is also impossible — that would require the key, and with the key on the server the whole point is lost. This is not a shortcoming; it is the terms of the deal.

Off-the-shelf systems usually offer a credential store where decryption happens on their side. That is more convenient and protects against a different threat model. Choosing between the two approaches means choosing what exactly you are protecting yourself from, and that choice, too, is yours to make.

sections.heading: Deletion that doesn't delete straight away
body: The "delete" button in a record-keeping system should almost never delete immediately. People make mistakes, and a project deleted by accident along with its correspondence is a loss that nothing can make up for.

The standard solution is soft deletion: the record is marked as deleted and disappears from the lists. It has a side effect people forget about: if nothing ever deletes such records for real, they pile up forever and end up in every nightly backup. For client contacts, this directly contradicts Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, which expects personal data to be deleted once the purpose of processing it has been served.

So for us, deletion is a thirty-day grace period, not a graveyard: for a month the record can be restored from the trash, after which a daily job erases it for good. Notes are deleted together with the record, not before — otherwise a restored project would come back without its discussion, which is almost as bad as not coming back at all.

sections.heading: Statuses don't remind anyone of anything
body: The most common reason a deal is lost is not the lack of a CRM but a card quietly sitting in the status "in correspondence" for the fourth month running. A status cannot remind anyone of itself: it describes a state, not a commitment.

That is why the main field on our leads is not the status but the next step: a date and one line saying exactly what needs to be done. An overdue next step is the only thing that puts a lead on the main screen and into the morning digest. The line of description matters as much as the date: the reminder "call about the estimate — 3 days overdue" is clear without opening the card, while a bare "lead overdue" forces you to open it and try to remember.

The digest arrives in the team chat in the morning — and doesn't arrive at all if there is nothing to remind anyone of. A daily "all clear" teaches people not to open the bot, and then one day they scroll past something important.
Almost every off-the-shelf system has a reminder mechanism. The question is whether it is mandatory: if the "next step" field can be left empty, it will be left empty.

sections.heading: What a custom CRM costs
body: With us, CRM development starts at {price:400000} and four weeks — that is a system on a ready-made architecture with the core modules, roles, basic integrations and data migration. Processes built to fit, dashboards, integrations with services and telephony, and team training start at {price:700000} and eight weeks. A complex platform with access rights split by department and designed for high load starts at {price:1200000} and twelve weeks.

To this you have to honestly add what usually doesn't make it into the development estimate. Changes after launch — in the first months the system changes constantly, because real work always differs from what was described at the start. Hosting and backups. Dependency and security updates. And the most expensive item — the availability of people who can make changes.
It is worth budgeting around 15–20% of the development cost per year for support. Less than that means the system will age and one day need not changes but a rewrite.

sections.heading: What an off-the-shelf system costs over three years
body: The cost of an off-the-shelf system is almost always calculated from the licence price, and that is almost always wrong. You need to add up four things.

The subscription — usually per user per month, and it grows with the team. Implementation — setting up pipelines, permissions and templates and importing data; that is separate work done by an integrator. Customisation — everything that can't be set up with checkboxes and needs modules or scripts; over time this is the least predictable line item. And migration — the cost of leaving if you ever decide to go.

The last item is the one people notice last. Data in an off-the-shelf system can be exported, but it is exported in that system's model: deals with stages, fields with internal names, files as a separate archive. The links between entities and the process logic aren't exported at all, because they live in the settings. The longer and more deeply you are in the system, the more it costs to leave.

Over a one-year horizon, off-the-shelf is almost always cheaper. Over three to five years, for a team that actively customises the system, the gap narrows and sometimes flips. There is no universal answer here — there is arithmetic worth doing with your own numbers.

sections.heading: The hybrid that is most often what you need
body: The "custom or off-the-shelf" opposition is false more often than it seems. The option that works is usually in the middle: the off-the-shelf CRM stays where it is strong — the pipeline, calls, correspondence, the mobile app — and alongside it you add your own services for whatever doesn't fit its model.

A client or partner portal with your own calculation logic. Production or field work tracking. A dashboard for a department that needs something other than what the CRM shows. Pricing by your own formula. All of this lives separately and exchanges data with the CRM through an integration.

This approach has a price — synchronisation. Two systems sharing data will inevitably drift apart unless you decide in advance which one is the master for each entity. The rule is simple and non-negotiable: every entity has exactly one owner, and the others read. A client is created in the CRM and the portal reads it; an order is created in the portal and the CRM reads it. As soon as both sides start writing to the same field, manual reconciliation begins.
In return, there is less development, the ceiling goes away, and you don't have to move anywhere.

sections.heading: How to choose: a short checklist
body: Off-the-shelf is enough if your process is enquiries, calls and deals; if the team is up to 15–20 people; if you need to start within the next few weeks; if you are not prepared to fund development on an ongoing basis.

A custom system is worth considering if the key entity of your business isn't called a "deal" and can't be represented as one without stretching; if half your data lives in custom fields and unwritten agreements; if reports are calculated in Excel anyway; if data cannot leave your infrastructure because of client or regulatory requirements; if you are already paying an integrator so much that the three-year total is comparable to development.
And separately: if you can't describe your process on one page, neither system will help. Automating an undescribed process gives you an undescribed process that now also has a database.

sections.heading: When you don't need a custom CRM
body: You don't need one if the main problem is discipline, not the tool. A system won't make anyone call; it will only show that nobody did.

You don't need one if the process changes every month. Development fixes the process in code, and fixing something that hasn't settled yet means rewriting it. At this stage an off-the-shelf system, or even a spreadsheet, is more useful.

You don't need one if nobody is going to be responsible for it. A system needs an owner inside the company — not a developer, but someone who decides how things should be. Without one, any CRM, custom or off-the-shelf, turns into a dumping ground of cards within six months.

And you don't need one if you haven't tried an off-the-shelf system yet. A month of working in a boxed product gives you a list of specific complaints, and that is the best specification you can bring to a developer. Without it, development starts with guesswork.

sections.heading: Where to start
body: Describe the one process that hurts most on a single page: who does what, in what order and what counts as the result. See whether it maps onto the entities of an off-the-shelf system without stretching. If it does, take the off-the-shelf one and come back to this question in a year. If it doesn't, you already know exactly what needs to be developed, and the conversation with a contractor won't start from scratch.

We do both: we design custom CRMs and platforms, and we connect the missing services to existing systems. If you're not sure which path is yours, write to us — we'll go through your process and tell you honestly if an off-the-shelf system will do.
