body: A parser is just about the only kind of program that breaks not because something was changed in it, but because something changed outside it. The supplier changed the header in the price list, the website updated its layout, a new field appeared in the database, and collection that worked yesterday returns nothing today or, worse, rubbish.

You can't avoid this entirely, but you can make sure a breakdown isn't a disaster. The first measure is checking the result on the way in, not on the way out. The parser knows what to expect: if forty rows arrive from a price list of ten thousand, if a price turns negative, if half the columns disappear, it stops and reports the problem instead of loading corrupted data into the production database.

The second is alerts. A silent failure is worse than a loud one: the data quietly goes stale, and you find out a week later from a customer complaint. So the parser logs every run to monitoring and sends a notification to Telegram or by email if something goes wrong.

The third is anchoring to meaning, not position. A column in Excel is found by its header name, not its number; data on a page is found by stable attributes, not by a long chain of nesting that will break with any design change.
The fourth is keeping the source material. Downloaded files and pages are stored as they are, so when something fails you can see exactly what changed. Without this you are debugging blind.
The fifth is graceful degradation. If one optional field out of twenty fails to parse, it is better to write the other nineteen and flag the gap than to bring down the whole export.

sections.heading: Legal limits
body: Collecting publicly available data is lawful in itself, but there are limits, and it's worth knowing them before you start.

Personal data. Names, phone numbers, addresses and email addresses are personal data under Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, even if they are publicly available. Collecting them makes you a personal data operator, with all the obligations that follow. The rule is simple: if the task can be solved without personal data, solve it without.

Copyright. Texts, photographs and descriptions are protected by copyright regardless of how you obtained them. Collecting someone else's product descriptions for internal analytics and publishing them on your own website are fundamentally different things in the eyes of the law.

Terms of use and robots.txt. A robots.txt file isn't a legal document, but it expresses the owner's wishes, and ignoring it becomes an argument against you. A website's user agreement may explicitly prohibit automated collection, and that is already a contractual matter.
Load. Collection that interferes with someone else's service is a separate story, and it is closer to unlawful interference than to harmless reading of public pages.

The practical conclusion: collect only what the task really needs, don't touch personal data without a legal basis, don't publish other people's content as your own, and don't create load. In borderline cases it's cheaper to show the task to a lawyer than to sort things out afterwards.

sections.heading: How much it costs and how long it takes
body: The cost of a parser is determined not by the volume of data but by the number of exceptions. Collecting a million rows from tidy XML is easier and cheaper than collecting a thousand from a dozen messy Excel files with different structures.

Our guide figures are these. A simple parser with one source and export to a spreadsheet: from {price:50000}. A system with several sources, automatic scheduled collection and export to a database or CRM: from {price:110000}. Complex cases with protected sources, a resilient architecture and monitoring: from {price:220000}.

As for timelines: a simple parser usually takes one to two weeks, regular collection from several sources two to four weeks, and a large system with monitoring from a month and a half. Most of this time goes not into code but into working through exceptions in the real data.

What affects the price most: the number of sources and the variety of their formats; whether a headless browser is needed; how dirty the source data is; whether reference data has to be matched; how often it updates and what reliability is required. That's why we don't name a figure from a description of the task: first we look at the real files or pages, and only then do we estimate.

And a fair warning: a parser needs ongoing support. Sources change, and every few months something has to be fixed. A one-off build without support is a saving that ends with the data quietly ceasing to update six months later.

sections.heading: Example: a catalogue of 100,000 items
body: One of our projects was an online shop selling spare parts for heavy machinery. The task was to fill the catalogue: around a hundred thousand items from the supplier, with part numbers, specifications, prices and the machine assemblies they belong to.

There's no way to do this by hand: even at one minute per item it comes to more than a year of one person's work. We collected the data automatically, brought part numbers and names to a single format, matched the product range against the internal reference data and set up regular price and stock updates, so the catalogue wouldn't go out of date the day after launch.

The main work, as usual, was not in collection but in normalisation: the same product had different names at the supplier and at the client, some specifications were written into the general text description, and some part numbers differed only in letter case and spaces.
The result is a catalogue in which customers find the part they need themselves, instead of phoning to check availability.

sections.heading: How we work
body: We start with real data: we ask you to send sample files, access to a test database or links to the pages. We don't give an estimate based on a description of the task: too often the description and the actual content differ.

Next we design: which fields are needed, how to match them with your reference data, how often to update, where to export, what to do if something fails. Then we build and launch collection with monitoring, so you hear about a problem from the system rather than from a customer.
We deliver the result where it is used: a spreadsheet, a database, a CRM or an API exchange with your system, with no manual copying in between.

takeaways: Parsing covers three different jobs: breaking down files, extracting data from databases and collecting it from websites.
The time goes not into reading the format but into handling exceptions: broken encodings, merged cells, scans instead of text.
If a source has an API or an official export, it is always better than parsing the markup.
We don't get around anti-collection protection: if a source is deliberately closed, we look for a legal route to the same data.
A parser must check its results and report failures: a silent breakdown is worse than a loud one.
Personal data falls under 152-FZ even when it is publicly available.
